The `rust-crypto` crate has not seen a release or GitHub commit since 2016,
and its author is unresponsive.

*NOTE: The (old) `rust-crypto` crate (with hyphen) should not be confused with

advisory.details:
### Impact

The affected functions set environment variables without synchronization. On Unix-like operating systems, this can crash in multithreaded programs. Programs may segfault due to dereferencing a dangling pointer if an environment variable is read in a different thread than the affected functions. This may occur without the user's knowledge, notably in the Rust standard library or third-party libraries.

The affected functions from time 0.2.7 through 0.2.22 are:

- `time::UtcOffset::local_offset_at`
- `time::UtcOffset::try_local_offset_at`
- `time::UtcOffset::current_local_offset`
- `time::UtcOffset::try_current_local_offset`
- `time::OffsetDateTime::now_local`
- `time::OffsetDateTime::try_now_local`

The affected functions in time 0.1 (all versions) are:

- `time::at_utc`
- `time::at`
- `time::now`
- `time::tzset`

Non-Unix targets (including Windows and wasm) are unaffected.

### Patches

Pending a proper fix, the internal method that determines the local offset has been modified to always return `None` on the affected operating systems. This has the effect of returning an `Err` on the `try_*` methods and `UTC` on the non-`try_*` methods.

Users and library authors with time in their dependency tree should perform `cargo update`, which will pull in the updated, unaffected code.

Users of time 0.1 do not have a patch and should upgrade to an unaffected version: time 0.2.23 or greater or the 0.3 series.

### Workarounds

A possible workaround for crates affected through the transitive dependency in `chrono`, is to avoid using the default `oldtime` feature dependency of the `chrono` crate by disabling its `default-features` and manually specifying the required features instead.

#### Examples:

`Cargo.toml`:  

```toml
chrono = { version = "0.4", default-features = false, features = ["serde"] }
```

```toml
chrono = { version = "0.4.22", default-features = false, features = ["clock"] }
```

Commandline:  

```bash
cargo add chrono --no-default-features -F clock
```

Sources:  
 - [chronotope/chrono#602 (comment)](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/issues/602#issuecomment-1242149249)  
 - [vityafx/serde-aux#21](https://github.com/vityafx/serde-aux/issues/21)

enrichments.details:
### Impact

Unix-like operating systems may segfault due to dereferencing a dangling pointer in specific circumstances. This requires an environment variable to be set in a different thread than the affected functions. This may occur without the user's knowledge, notably in a third-party library.

The affected functions from time 0.2.7 through 0.2.22 are:

- `time::UtcOffset::local_offset_at`
- `time::UtcOffset::try_local_offset_at`
- `time::UtcOffset::current_local_offset`
- `time::UtcOffset::try_current_local_offset`
- `time::OffsetDateTime::now_local`
- `time::OffsetDateTime::try_now_local`

The affected functions in time 0.1 (all versions) are:

- `at`
- `at_utc`
- `now`

Non-Unix targets (including Windows and wasm) are unaffected.

### Patches

In some versions of `time`, the internal method that determines the local offset has been modified to always return `None` on the affected operating systems. This has the effect of returning an `Err` on the `try_*` methods and `UTC` on the non-`try_*` methods. In later versions, `time` will attempt to determine the number of threads running in the process. If the process is single-threaded, the call will proceed as its safety invariant is upheld.

Users and library authors with time in their dependency tree must perform `cargo update`, which will pull in the updated, unaffected code.

Users of time 0.1 do not have a patch and must upgrade to an unaffected version: time 0.2.23 or greater or the 0.3 series.

### Workarounds

Library authors must ensure that the program only has one running thread at the time of calling any affected method. Binary authors may do the same and/or ensure that no other thread is actively mutating the environment.

### References

[time-rs/time#293](https://github.com/time-rs/time/issues/293).

In Rust time crate from version 0.2.7 and before version 0.2.23, unix-like operating systems may segfault due to dereferencing a dangling pointer in specific circumstances. This requires the user to set any environment variable in a different thread than the affected functions. The affected functions are time::UtcOffset::local_offset_at, time::UtcOffset::try_local_offset_at, time::UtcOffset::current_local_offset, time::UtcOffset::try_current_local_offset, time::OffsetDateTime::now_local and time::OffsetDateTime::try_now_local. Non-Unix targets are unaffected. This includes Windows and wasm. The issue was introduced in version 0.2.7 and fixed in version 0.2.23. En el crate time de Rust desde la versión 0.2.7 y anterior a versión 0.2.23, los sistemas operativos tipo Unix pueden segregarse debido a la desreferenciación de un puntero colgante en circunstancias específicas. Esto requiere que el usuario configure cualquier variable de entorno en un hilo diferente al de las funciones afectadas. Las funciones afectadas son time::UtcOffset::local_offset_at, time::UtcOffset::try_local_offset_at, time::UtcOffset::current_local_offset, time::UtcOffset::try_current_local_offset, time::OffsetDateTime::now_local y time::OffsetDateTime::try_now_local. Los objetivos que no son Unix no están afectados. Esto incluye Windows y wasm. El problema se introdujo en la versión 0.2.7 y se corrigió en la versión 0.2.23

enrichments.details: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 0.6.0 until 9.0.0, the AES entry reader in src/aes.rs verifies its HMAC only when the attacker-controlled data counter reaches zero. If the underlying bounded reader reaches the real end of the archive while data_remaining is still positive, or if an encrypted entry has no payload, the reader can return a clean end of stream without reading and comparing the authentication tag. Applications using by_index_decrypt, by_name_decrypt, by_path_decrypt, or password-enabled by_index_with_options can therefore accept modified plaintext without an authentication error. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.

enrichments.details: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 5.1.0 until 9.0.0, applications built with the legacy-zip feature can reserve output capacity from an attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed size before validating the compressed stream. The ShrinkDecoder path in src/legacy/shrink.rs can panic with a capacity overflow during ZipArchive::extract, and the Reduce and Implode decoders contain the same unbounded preallocation pattern. An unhandled panic can terminate an archive-processing service. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.

enrichments.details: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. Through 9.0.4, ZipArchive treats Central Directory File Header filenames as authoritative while ZipStreamReader extracts using Local File Header filenames without reconciling the duplicate metadata in src/read/stream.rs. A crafted archive can therefore appear benign to a component that inspects the central directory but cause a streaming extractor to write a different attacker-selected path and content, potentially overwriting files used by a downstream service. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.5.

advisory.details:
The `zip` crate preserves privileged Unix permission bits (SUID, SGID, and sticky bits) from ZIP `external_attributes` during extraction, instead of masking them to safe permission bits. If a privileged process (for example, `root` in an installer, CI/CD pipeline, or container build) extracts an attacker-controlled ZIP archive using `ZipArchive::extract()` or the stream extraction API, files can be created as setuid-root or setgid. This behavior allows the creation of SUID/SGID files during extraction, which can lead to local privilege escalation depending on the execution environment.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-vv5m-jxxh-4627
Cargo patched constraints (OR): >=9.0.0

advisory.details:
In `zip` 9.0.0-pre2, `ZipArchive::extract` creates a symbolic link from an archive entry after validating only the output entry path. The link target bytes are passed directly to the platform symlink API, so a malicious archive can create an entry inside the destination that resolves to an attacker-chosen path outside it. This behavior was verified on macOS and Linux. On either platform, a subsequent application read or write through that extracted entry accesses the external target with the extracting process's permissions.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4v9h-p7m9-rh26
Cargo patched constraints (OR): >=9.0.0

`ZipStreamReader::extract()` applies Unix permissions through extracted symlinks without validating the symlink target stays within the destination

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4684-h2q9-2vcp
Cargo patched constraints (OR): >=9.0.0

`ZipArchive::extract()` sizes the symlink-target buffer from the uncompressed
size declared in the central directory record, before reading a single byte of
entry data:

```rust
let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize);
```

Both inputs are attacker-controlled. `ZipFile::size()` returns
`uncompressed_size` verbatim from the central directory, widened to a full `u64`
by a ZIP64 extended-information extra field, and is never cross-checked against
the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate
bound for a symlink target. `ZipFile::is_symlink()` is decided entirely by the
`S_IFLNK` bit of the external-attributes field.

`Vec::with_capacity()` is infallible: when the reservation is refused it calls
`handle_alloc_error()` and aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic. It is
not caught by `catch_unwind()`, is unaffected by `panic = "unwind"`, and is not
contained by running the call on a worker thread.

A 112-byte archive is sufficient. One `Stored` entry flagged `S_IFLNK` with a
ZIP64 field declaring `uncompressed_size = 2^62` and a zero-byte payload makes
`extract()` fail with:

```
memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134
```

The declared value only needs to exceed the host's address space, not its RAM:
`Vec::with_capacity()` maps address space without touching pages, so resident
memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself. Under
a `ulimit -v` cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far
enough that a plain 32-bit `uncompressed_size` with no ZIP64 field suffices.

Applications that extract archives from untrusted input are affected on Unix and
Windows targets with default features and no special configuration: upload
handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup
restore and container-image layer extraction. No confidentiality or integrity
property is affected: there is no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no
disclosure and no data corruption.

The fix landed in [zip-rs/zip2#984](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/pull/984) and
shipped in 9.0.0.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3
Cargo patched constraints (OR): >=9.0.0

enrichments.details:
### Summary

The symbolic-link branch of `ZipArchive::extract_internal()` allocates a buffer using an attacker-declared size before reading any entry data. A 112-byte archive terminates the extracting process with `SIGABRT` through this infallible allocation.

### Details

```rust
#[cfg(any(unix, windows))]
if file.is_symlink() {
    let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize); // @audit unbounded memory allocation
    file.read_to_end(&mut target)?;
    drop(file);
    make_symlink(&outpath, &target, &self.shared.files)?;
    continue;
}
```

[`src/read/mod.rs#L399-L405`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/mod.rs#L399-L405) (reviewed commit `6f09b306`); the same code is at [`src/read.rs#L417-L418`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/v8.6.0/src/read.rs#L417-L418) in released v8.6.0.

Both inputs are attacker-controlled:

- [`ZipFile::size()`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zipfile.rs#L243-L246) returns `uncompressed_size` verbatim from the central directory record. A ZIP64 extended-information extra field widens it to a full `u64` ([`src/read/mod.rs#L619-L625`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/mod.rs#L619-L625)). It is never cross-checked against the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate bound for a symlink target.
- [`ZipFile::is_symlink()`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zipfile.rs#L256-L260) is decided entirely by the central directory's external-attributes field, via the `S_IFLNK` bit.

**Memory allocation failure → uncatchable process abort.** The reservation is sized from the declared `uncompressed_size` before a single byte of the entry is read. `Vec::with_capacity()` is infallible: on allocator refusal it calls `handle_alloc_error()`, which aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic — it is not caught by `catch_unwind()`, is unaffected by `panic = "unwind"`, and is not contained by isolating the call in a worker thread. This was verified by wrapping the call in all three at once; the process still died with exit 134.

The declared value needed is a property of the host's address space, not of reachability. On a 64 GB host with heuristic overcommit, declared sizes from roughly `2^38` upward abort reliably. Sizes at or above `2^63` instead trip `Vec`'s internal capacity check and produce a *catchable* `capacity overflow` panic, so an attacker simply avoids that band. The reproducer declares `2^62`, which exceeds the 47-bit user address space of x86-64 Linux outright and therefore aborts deterministically regardless of installed RAM or overcommit policy. Under a `ulimit -v` cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far enough that a plain 32-bit `uncompressed_size` with no ZIP64 field suffices — a virtual-memory limit lowers the bar rather than mitigating the defect.

This is process termination, not memory exhaustion: `Vec::with_capacity()` only maps address space and never touches pages, so resident memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself, before any byte is read.

### PoC

The reproducer consists of the following `zip` harness and payload. It requires only the `zip` crate; use a standard Base64 decoder to materialise the archive before running it.

```toml
[package]
name = "zip-poc"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
zip = "8.6.0"
```

```rust
use std::{env, fs::File, io::BufReader};

fn main() {
    let archive_path = env::args().nth(1).expect("usage: poc <archive.zip>");
    let outdir = std::env::temp_dir().join("zip-poc");
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&outdir).unwrap();

    let file = File::open(archive_path).unwrap();
    let mut archive = zip::ZipArchive::new(BufReader::new(file)).unwrap();
    let r = archive.extract(&outdir);            // <-- process dies here
    println!("SURVIVED: {:?}", r);
}
```

Save the Base64 payload below as `archive.b64`, remove its whitespace, decode it with a standard Base64 decoder (for example, `base64 -d archive.b64 > archive.zip` on Linux), and run `cargo run --release -- archive.zip`.

**Uncatchable abort — 112 bytes.** One `Stored` entry named `a`; external attributes `0xA1FF0000` (`S_IFLNK|0777`); ZIP64 extra field declaring `uncompressed_size = 2^62`; zero-byte payload. sha256 `0c68c3934f22651a6bd2726f7d58140124b1839196a1d0ae468864cdfda74676`.

```
UEsDBC0AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAP////8BAAAAYVBLAQItAy0AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAP//
//8BAAwAAAAAAAAAAAD/oQAAAABhAQAIAAAAAAAAAABAUEsFBgAAAAABAAEAOwAAAB8AAAAAAA==
```

Observed on x86-64 Linux, rustc 1.93.1, release profile, against both the reviewed commit and released v8.6.0:

```
entries=1
memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134
```

The `SURVIVED` line never prints. Wrapping `extract()` in `catch_unwind` inside a spawned thread with `panic = "unwind"` produces the identical outcome.

### Impact

Applications running on Unix or Windows targets that call `ZipArchive::extract()` on attacker-supplied input are affected, with default features and no special configuration. The malicious 112-byte archive causes an unrecoverable, uncatchable termination of the extracting process, repeatable at will and not mitigable at the call site with `catch_unwind`, a worker thread, or a pre-flight metadata check.

Upload handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup restore and container-image layer extraction all match this pattern. No confidentiality or integrity property is affected: no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no disclosure and no data corruption.

### Suggested remediation

Before allocating, compare `file.size()` with a documented, platform-appropriate maximum symlink-target length and reject entries that exceed it. Alternatively, replace `Vec::with_capacity()` with fallible `try_reserve()` and return an I/O error when allocation fails. Do not use Linux's `PATH_MAX` as a cross-platform contract.

Apply the allocation fix to `src/read/stream.rs` as defence-in-depth, although its symlink path is currently unreachable because streaming entries have no symlink attributes.

For reference, the crate already applies exactly this defence to another untrusted size on the same path: `ZipArchive::new()` clamps a suspicious `number_of_files` to zero and explicitly rejects an oversized central directory before reserving ([`src/read/zip_archive.rs#L185-L202`](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/blob/6f09b3064ec87c3a69ea9f3413f9f9638b4aa446/src/read/zip_archive.rs#L185-L202)). The symlink branch received neither guard. A survey of `Vec::with_capacity` across `src/` finds exactly two sites sized from untrusted input: `src/read/mod.rs:401` and `src/read/stream.rs:73`.

zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 1.3.0 until 9.0.0, ZipArchive::extract in src/read/mod.rs calls Vec::with_capacity for a symbolic link target using the attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed_size before reading entry data. A small archive can request an impossible capacity, causing the infallible allocation path to abort the process before the entry is validated. The failure cannot be contained with catch_unwind or a worker thread, allowing repeated denial of service in archive-processing applications. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.
